test: Compute days late per paid invoice (payment day - due_day, operating days) and overdue dollar-days per customer. Check concentration (share of overdue dollar-days held by top 1%/10% of customers), persistence (rank correlation of customer lateness year to year; share of top-decile customers staying top-decile), relation to terms_days, credit_limit, trade, payment method (check vs ACH), and check whether due_day is built in calendar days against operating-day payment days (artefact). Size the financing cost of overdue balance from average overdue dollars outstanding.
support: Top 10% of customers hold >50% of overdue dollar-days, customer lateness correlates strongly year to year, lateness is unrelated to or rises with terms/credit limit, and lateness is not explained by method.
weaken: Lateness is spread roughly in proportion to sales, days late is short and near-uniform, customer lateness is uncorrelated across years (random), or 'late' depends mechanically on how due_day is computed (e.g. calendar days of terms added as operating days).
expect: Given how synthetic and clean the payment data looks (61% late flat every year), I expect lateness to be largely random per invoice, concentration roughly tracking revenue (top 10% holding about what their sales share is), and weak persistence. Moderate confidence (~60%) that the hypothesis is weakened; possibly a due_day artefact or a terms-dependent pattern.
